The DPA fined a genomics and biotechnology company €2.4 million for failing to adequately protect sensitive genetic and health data and for notifying the DPA about a personal data breach after the 72-hour deadline.
The DPA fined a controller €60,000 for failing to comply with a corrective order requiring it to formalise and report its relationship with a processor.

The Spanish DPA examined 191 complaints (162 after leaving out 29 with faulty data) about marketing calls, SMS and emails made on behalf of Vodafone España, including to people who had opted out or were on advertising exclusion (Robinson) lists. It found that Vodafone failed to control its processors (Arts. 28 and 24 GDPR), made international transfers in breach of Art. 44 GDPR, breached Art. 21 LSSICE on commercial electronic communications, and breached Art. 48.1.b LGT read with Art. 21 GDPR and Art. 23 LOPDGDD on the right to object to unwanted calls. It imposed four fines (EUR 4,000,000, 2,000,000, 150,000 and 2,000,000, EUR 8,150,000 in total) and ordered Vodafone to bring its processing into line with the GDPR and LOPDGDD within six months.

A former customer complained that a CaixaBank group consumer finance entity had queried solvency files about him and included him in a pre-approved credit campaign although he was no longer a customer. The AEPD opened investigations into how the entity profiles customers for commercial purposes. It found that the consent-gathering procedures for profiling lacked a valid legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR. It fined CaixaBank Payments & Consumer EUR 3,000,000 and ordered it to bring its consent procedures for commercial profiling into line with data protection law within six months.

The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) fined a politician €1000 for unsolicited political communication (SMS) without consent or any other legal basis, according to the national provisions on unsolicited communications.

The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) fined a politician €2000 for unsolicited political communication (email) without consent or any other legal basis according to the national provisions on unsolicited communications.

The UK DPA fined a controller approximately €200,000 (£170,000) for contacting almost 200,000 individuals who had registered their intent not to receive marketing calls with the Telephone Preference Service ('TPS'). In particular, the controller had failed to check datasets purchased from 11 third-party data providers against the TPS.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) decided not to take further actions over the Department for Digital, Culture, Media & Sport (DCMS) for its management of a UK citizen's (the complainant) request of information on which articles of the (now repealed) Directive 95/46/EC, according to the European Commission, had not been properly implemented by the UK government at the (now repealed) Data Protection Act 1998.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On 6 February 2020, ICO adopted a decision, stating that the Northamptonshire Police acted lawfully by refusing to confirm or deny whether it held information requested by the complainant. However, ICO found that the Northamptonshire Police’s failure to specify the exemption on which it was relying constituted a breach. These conclusions were made based on the relevant provisions of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 ("FOIA"), Data Protection Act 2018 and the General Data Protection regulation ("GDPR").

The DPA fined a company €5,320 for a failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures in connection with the destruction of employees' personal data contained in paper documents. Discarded documents were left unsecured and accessible to anyone.
An employer (data controller) accessed emails and forwarded them from the account of an employee who was on prolonged absence, thus violating Article 5 (a) and (c) & Article 6 GDPR.
A high school was issued a warning for violating Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, because it disclosed a printed list with grades and personal information.

The Slovenian DPA (IP) issued an opinion that employers cannot collect or process employee's COVID-19 test results or their health card number unless required to do so by sectoral regulation. Even where such regulations are in place, the employer must prove that their data collection practices comply with the principle of data minimization.
The Slovenian DPA found that a controller failed to provide clear and consistent information about its use of cookies.

The Slovenian DPA issued an advisory opinion on the establishment of a temporary information system for the combat against the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic to the government of the Republic of Slovenia and the Jozef Stefan Institute.
The Slovenian DPA stated that it is allowed to make public only those minutes of the parent council meetings that contain public information.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On 14 February the Informacijski pooblaščenec of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided a non-binding opinion pursuant to Article 58(3) GDPR. The IP pronounced itself on the use of drones.

<!--Here the main article starts--> The Informacijski pooblaščenec, Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided an opinion pursuant to Article 58 GDPR. The subject matter of the opinion regarded processing of personal data in an employment context.

<!--Here the main article starts--> On 14 February the Informacijski pooblaščenec, Information Commissioner of the Republic of Slovenia (IP), provided a non-binding opinion pursuant to Article 58 GDPR. The subject matter of the opinion regarded the legality of installing an automatic camera for the purpose of monitoring recreational activities on watercourses in the Triglay National Park (TNP). The IP refrained from commenting in the particular, but highlighted areas which required a closer look by the park.
The Slovenian DPA stated that the director (CEO) or member of the management of the company shall not be a DPO.

The DPA held that the Farmers’ Association published data concerning registration and ownership of horses in a public database and lawfully licensed this data to the provider of an app for horse owners. According to the DPA, this was necessary for the public interest.

The DPA issued a reprimand against an employee of a hospital for conducting unauthorised searches of a data subjects medical records. The DPA considered the employee to be a controller because they exceeded their access privileges.
The DPA reprimanded an airport operator for informing data subjects inadequately and too late about the usage of CCTV and licence plate monitoring in its airport car parks.

The Icelandic DPA (Persónuvernd) has ruled that the National Commissioner of Police had been allowed to refuse to give information about which employees looked up complainant's personal data in the case file system, LÖKE. However, the Commissioner was requested to provide information about which responsible parties were looking for complainant's personal data.

The Icelandic DPA issued an advisory opinion clarifying the interplay between the Information Act and the Privacy Act which implements the GDPR in Iceland. The DPA clarified that the information in question is personal data and that processing of personal data requires a legal ground as per Article 6 GDPR.

<!--Here the main article starts--> Persónuvernd decided on a case concerning a list of employee’s sick leave put up in a hotel kitchen. A list of absences was hung up in a space accessible to all of the hotel’s employees. While the registration of sick leave was covered by sectorial labor law, and thus had a legal basis under Article 9 GDPR, the security of processing was not ensured following Article 5 (1)(f).

<!--Here the main article starts--> A person filed a complaint with the Finnish Data Protection Authority (Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto) regarding not being notified that a sales call had been recorded and being denied access to recording of the call. The Tietosuojavaltuutetun toimisto found that the company’s procedure to record calls did not fulfil the requirements under Article 5(1)(a), 12(1) and 13 GDPR. The decision highlighted that audio is personal data when it is stored and it is possible to identify an individual. As such, companies must inform data subjects when they collect the information. In addition, data subjects have the right to receive a copy of the call. The Data Protection Authority therefore ordered the company to modify its processing operation pursuant to Article 58(2)(d) GDPR.

The Data Protection Authority of Finland instructed a debt collection agency to delete personal data pursuant to the request of the data subject. According to applicable obligations arising from the Finnish Accounting Act, the personal data concerned should not to be retained.

The Court upheld the decision of the Municipal Court, which clarified that data subjects do not have legal standing to challenge the outcome of administrative proceedings, however may challenge DPA’s decisions which concern their specific complaints.
